items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: JUST IN: 2 areas are now being monitored for possible tropical development by the National Hurricane Center! The remnants of Tropical Storm Dolly are several hundred miles east of the Leeward Islands and moving quickly west to west-northwest around 25 mph. Redevelopment is possible, but unlikely, with just 10% chance of formation over the next 7-days. Regardless of development, Dolly’s remnants could bring locally heavy rain and gusty winds to the Leeward Islands, U.S. Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico over the next several days. Closer to 'home', a weak area of low pressure in the northeastern and north-central Gulf is producing disorganized showers and clouds. It should remain nearly stationary for the next several days and any development is expected to be slow. The National Hurricane Center also gives this system a 10% chance of development over the next 7-days. Neither system is an immediate major development concern but both areas will be worth monitoring over the coming days🌀🌀🌴

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: TROPICAL STORM DOLLY🌀🌴has fallen apart and is no longer a Tropical Storm but the remnants are worthy of monitoring! Tropical Storm Dolly formed Thursday over the central tropical Atlantic, becoming the 4th named Storm of the 2026 Atlantic Hurricane Season. Shortly after forming, Dolly’s circulation quickly unraveled as it encountered a hostile environment with strong wind shear and dry air. Dolly’s remnants will continue moving west toward the eastern Caribbean this weekend bringing the potential for gusty winds and some rain to the northern-end of the Lesser Antilles, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Beyond the Caribbean, there is high uncertainty as to what happens to the remnants next week. A possible scenario takes the disturbance west toward the eastern Gulf while another eventually curves the system northward near the Bahamas and then offshore of the Southeast Coast as remnants - not as a Tropical Storm. There is also high uncertainty over whether the remnants will be able to reorganize. Environmental conditions initially will not be favorable for redevelopment; however, could become somewhat more favorable the farther west or north it travels but redevelopment is NOT guaranteed. The key point to take away is that there is NO immediate reason for concern along the Gulf or Southeast Coast but interests from the Gulf Coast to the Southeast should continue to monitor the forecast over the coming days. The eventual track and any potential for redevelopment will become clearer over the coming days🌀🌴

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: SOUTHWEST MONSOON SURGE⛈️🌵🌧️a much more active monsoon pattern is expected to develop across the Southwest beginning today and continuing through the weekend into next week! After the recent stretch of intense heat and more limited storm coverage, the atmospheric setup is becoming increasingly favorable for a broader return of thunderstorms. The biggest change will be the subtropical ridge shifting eastward toward Texas and Oklahoma with a developing trough off the West Coast. This will place the Southwest beneath deeper southeast to southerly flow, allowing a significant increase in monsoon moisture. Atmospheric moisture is forecast to climb to roughly 125-150% of normal with precipitable water values potentially reaching 1.6-1.8 inches by Saturday and remaining elevated through much of the weekend, into next week. Thunderstorm coverage should respond quickly to the moisture increase. As deeper moisture returns, flash flooding will become an increasing concern, especially with thunderstorms capable of producing locally heavy rainfall. Strong to potentially damaging thunderstorm wind gusts will remain another concern Not everyone will see storms each day, and the monsoon often features more active and less active days depending on smaller-scale disturbances and leftover outflow boundaries. However, the overall environment appears considerably more favorable for widespread activity than what we've seen recently⛈️🌵🌧️

The remnants of #Dolly are still being tracked, and a few models are suggesting the system could potentially get its act together again late this week into next weekend.

Does that mean we’re getting Dolly: Act II?

Hell if I know. It’s hurricane season and the atmosphere does whatever it wants.

For now, nothing to worry about. This is firmly in the “Hmm… let’s keep an eye on those schmuck remnants.”

We’ll watch it this week and see if more models join the party… or if the GFS and Canadian quietly delete the evidence and act like they never said a word.

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
Many of you have asked how my hand is doing, so here’s an update!

I’m now four weeks post-surgery, and it’s healing extremely well. In fact, I haven’t had any pain for weeks. Of course, no pain doesn’t mean it’s 100% healed. Broken bones take time, so I’m still being careful and following the rules which include wearing the splint when moving around and sleeping. 

Luckily, I’ve been in great hands (no pun intended) with the Occupational Therapy team at OrthoSC These three rockstars, from left to right, are Sonya, Liz and Kathy.

Liz, in particular, has been amazing. She’s been gradually working with me to get my hand back to normal while also taking great care of the incision area to minimize scarring. I couldn’t be happier with what she’s done for me.

And maybe just as important, they play GREAT music during therapy! I actually look forward to my visits with these ladies. Thank you for taking such great care of me!

For those who don’t know how I broke it, it happened the Friday night before Mom passed away. It was an incredibly difficult and emotional time. Mom’s health was failing, Dad wasn’t doing well, and in a moment of frustration and emotion, I punched a wall.

Unfortunately, I didn’t hit drywall. I found the stud. 

The stud won.

The result was a clean break of the fifth metacarpal in my hand and, ultimately, surgery. Definitely not one of my better decisions. But four weeks later, I’m very grateful to be healing so well and especially grateful for the people helping me get back to 100%.

items.text: FALL TEMPS TO RING IN THE ‘BER’ MONTH📉🍂🌧️❄️a notable pattern change is setting up across the Pacific Northwest and parts of the West, moving into the first week of September, bringing cooler temperatures and increased chances for precipitation! The main driver is a trough developing near the West Coast. This southward dip in the jet stream will be associated with cooler air aloft and lower atmospheric pressure, favoring cooler air being drawn southward into the region. The latest numerical guidance continues to show the Pacific Northwest has increased odds of below-normal temperatures with the cooler signal extending south through parts of the western Great Basin and into northern and central California. The trough will also strengthen onshore flow from the Pacific, allowing cooler, moisture-rich marine air to move inland. Chances for above-normal precipitation are elevated across parts of the West, with the Pacific Northwest favored to see wetter than normal conditions. This doesn't necessarily mean continuous rain or that every location will see significant rainfall. Rather, the overall pattern becomes more favorable for passing weather systems, showers and periods of wetter weather compared with what is typical. The increased cloud cover, precipitation and stronger marine influence should also help reinforce the cooler pattern. There’s also a chance for mountain snow for the Northwest. Meanwhile, it's almost the opposite story farther south and east. Strong ridging is expected to favor continued above-normal temperatures across much of the Southwest and Southern Plains📉🌧️❄️

Two weeks after the total solar eclipse, the Moon takes its turn in Earth's shadow.

On the night of August 27-28, a deep partial lunar eclipse darkens the Full Sturgeon Moon, with up to 96% of the lunar disk sliding into Earth's umbra, the dark central shadow. It falls just short of total, leaving a thin bright sliver along one edge, but the rest of the Moon will glow a deep coppery red. This is the most dramatic lunar eclipse anywhere on Earth until the total eclipse of December 31, 2028.

🔴 Greatest eclipse comes at 04:12 UTC on August 28, with the partial phase running from 02:33 to 05:52 UTC. The Americas and South America get the best views with the Moon high overhead; observers in Europe, Africa, and western Asia should find a clear western horizon as the Moon nears setting.

No equipment or eye protection needed. Just look up 🌕🔴

It's been fifteen years since Hurricane Irene made landfall as a strong Category 1 Hurricane near Cape Lookout, but the impacts from Irene are still apparent in parts of the Outer Banks in Dare and Hyde Counties, from altered land and infrastructure. 

The most iconic and disruptive impact was the storm surge from Pamlico Sound that crashed over the narrow strip of land on the Southern Outer Banks, tearing open multiple new inlets on Hatteras Island (including a massive 200+ foot breach at the Pea Island National Wildlife Refuge). This would effectively cut off Hatteras Island from the rest of the world. The roughly 2,500 residents on Hatteras Island were temporarily stranded, requiring emergency ferry service to deliver supplies and personnel. Impacts are still felt today on Pea Island. Over 800 homes and businesses on Ocracoke Island were flooded, and nearly 30% of all homes in Pamlico County were flooded. 15.74 inches of rain fell in Bayboro, and tropical storm-force winds extended over 200 miles from the center of Irene thanks to its large size. Half a million folks lost power. 

Do you remember Irene? 
-Ethan

TROPICAL UPDATE
5:30 PM THURSDAY 8/27/2026

Tropical Storm Dolly formed earlier today, but it’s likely to be a short-lived system. Dolly will run into a wall of strong wind shear this weekend, which should quickly take its toll.

It’s highly likely Dolly will weaken and eventually degenerate into a tropical wave, bringing gusty winds and some much-needed rainfall to drought-stricken Puerto Rico.

There’s been quite a bit of talk about whether Dolly’s remnants could reorganize once they reach an area of lighter wind shear early next week. However, given how much the system is expected to be torn apart by strong wind shear this weekend, redevelopment appears very unlikely. In fact, about 95% of the models and their ensemble members show Dolly never making a comeback.

And I’m perfectly OK with that!

Fall is just around the corner, but if you're in Central Florida, don't expect it to arrive quickly. 

I know the appearance of Halloween decorations in stores, PSLs & everything else pumpkin makes it seem like fall is just around the corner. 

Although meteorological fall is Sept, Oct & Nov, here in the Bay Area, we don't really start to feel "fall" until the month of October. Even then, it's really the second half of October that starts to see more noticeable reductions in temperatures & humidity levels. Highs in October usually stay in the 80s.

The real cool stuff, highs in the 70s, doesn't happen until November & lasts through the winter months. 

Until then, September doesn't usually see much, if any, "fall-like" weather, though a drop in the humidity later in the month is not unheard of, which can at least lead to cooler nights & mornings.

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: THE SEASONS ARE CHANGING📉🍂there is increasing confidence in a colder system bringing well-below-normal temperatures to parts of the Inland Northwest and Northern U.S. Rockies late next week into next weekend! The Climate Prediction Center has highlighted the region for an increased risk of much-below-normal temperatures from September 4-5 and the overall pattern is supported by forecast guidance showing a notable push of colder air into the Northwest and Northern Rockies. There’s also the potential for high-elevation snow, particularly across the Northern U.S. Rockies. Depending on the strength and track of the system, even some of the highest peaks of the Cascades could see light snow during this timeframe. It’s still a week+ away, so the exact magnitude of the cold and snow potential will need to be refined, but this could provide an early taste of fall - and perhaps even a touch of winter at the highest elevations❄️🍂🥶📉

items.text: Moisture associated with the remnants of Tropical Storm Iselle are being pulled north into California, bringing an increasing chance for isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms today and Friday! Of note, while the entire duration of this eclipse is quite long as the Moon traverses through Earth's shadow(s), many will find best viewing +/- 30 minutes from maximum eclipse. Happy viewing, it's going to be a few years before we get our next show of this caliber!

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: TROPICAL STORM ISELLE BRINGS MOISTURE TO CALIFORNIA BEGINNING TODAY🌀🌴🌧️ ⛈️a plume of deep tropical and subtropical moisture associated with the remnants of Tropical Storm Iselle are being pulled northward into California today and especially Friday as an upper-level trough approaches the West Coast! While this is not expected to be a widespread rain event, moisture levels will increase considerably and scattered showers and storms could develop across portions of the state. Today, tropical moisture begins spreading into Central and Southern California. There is around a low to medium chance for showers across portions of Southern California, the Central Coast and Bay Area while isolated activity will also be possible farther inland. Most locations will remain dry, but brief showers, sprinkles or virga could develop almost anywhere beneath the moisture plume. Thunderstorm chances today remain low but non-zero. The combination of tropical moisture, heat and instability means an isolated heavier shower or thunderstorm cannot be completely ruled out today. Gusty and erratic winds could also occur near showers or virga. The better opportunity for precipitation arrives Friday as the approaching Pacific Northwest trough taps directly into the subtropical moisture plume. Shower chances expand northward into the Sacramento Valley where much of the Valley now has a low to medium chance for rain showers. The Sierra Nevada should have the best opportunity for meaningful precipitation with thunderstorm probabilities increasing Friday. Localized flooding is possible in the Sierra Nevada. This is a classic low-probability, potentially higher-impact setup. Most Californians probably won't see measurable rain, but any isolated thunderstorm that develops within this unusually moist and unstable environment could produce locally heavier rain, lightning and gusty winds🌀🌴🌧️ ⛈️
